Satan is not invented. The term evolved from a generic word to a specific word, but the core principle is something intrinsic to reality itself. Specifically, a being that encapsulates the spiritual "will to harm" being exhibited with a false sanctimony.

The basic word שָׂטַן refers to an adversary. For example, in the Book of Numbers in the story of Balaam, we can see this generic use in reference to the angel who stopped Balaam's donkey. The angel is clearly working with God, not against God. It's only Balaam that thinks this angel is a "satan."

But over time it became used for a specific adversary and/or group of adversaries of the people of God. This particularization converged onto a specific being at some point. When we get to the Book of Job and Zechariah, we can see that Satan is no longer a generic term but the character is referred to as "the Satan." By the time of Jesus, it was simply a moniker for the same evil entity that went under the name Baalzebub. This "lord of the flies" which the eponymous book so aptly describes.

Because Jesus specifically speaks of Satan as a personal entity albeit one which can inhabit other individuals, most of us Christians understand that Satan is a personal entity. We certainly recognize that God has a "testing" character but it's a different kind of character than what Satan has with his legalism and temptation which attempt to destroy faith and good standing with God. God's "test" is never designed to destroy. God's "testing" nature can be described as the "well-intentioned trickster who wants to teach a difficult lesson." Satan's is the "rule mongering prosecutor who tricks others into incriminating themselves and being destroyed for it." Very different in terms of intention, although the latter is certainly something the former can utilize for various "teaching" goals.

Anyway, going back to "Lucifer." This word is a Latin translation of the Greek word Φωσφόρος/Ἑωσφόρος. (phosphoros) There are exactly 2 uses of this word in the Greek Bible. One in the Old Testament, the other in the New Testament. It's worth noting that another reference which is commonly lumped in with these is Revelation 22:16 where Jesus is called the "bright morning star" but that citation has a different Greek phrase: ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς ὁ πρωϊνός...

At any rate, the OT reference is from the LXX translation which produced the familiar Isaiah 14:12 "How art thou fallen from heaven O Lucifer son of the morning." The Greek word is itself translating the Hebrew words הֵילֵ֣ל בֶּן־שָׁ֑חַר (helel ben shachar) which was originally a Tyrian deity and it's being used to symbolize a King being deposed for evildoing. That "fallen" star has become a symbol of Satan by analogy with Jesus's statement "I saw Satan fall as lightning." (Luke 10:18) There's a similar citation in Ezekiel 28:14-16 about a fallen cherub which is also often linked to this verse allegorically.

The other citation in 2 Peter 1:19 where the word is translated "We also have the prophetic message as something completely reliable, and you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts." In this case, it's clearly a reference to the believer's spirit of faith.

In that case, we can deduce the actual usage of "light bearer" must be divided into the case of the "fallen light bearer" (one who had faith, but then turned away... like Satan) and the "un-fallen light bearer." (one who has integrity and keeps it)
